Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

LOS ANGELES (CNN) -- A group of anonymous software developers said they will soon start selling a program that will allow iPhone owners to use the hugely popular device on cell phone systems around the world and not just with AT&T. Apple's iPhone is yet to go on sale outside the U.S. Apple's iPhone, released in the United States two months ago, was engineered to operate for the first two years only on the AT&T system through an exclusive arrangement between Apple and AT&T. It has not yet been sold outside of the U.S. Los Angeles software consultant Brett Schulte, who is not affiliated with the developers, demonstrated the software for CNN Friday evening. An iPhone that had the new software appeared to work on the T-Mobile system just seconds after Schulte replaced the AT&T SIM card with a T-Mobile SIM card. "It's completely software hacked," Schulte said. "There's no case opening required. It's not required to do any kind of disassembly." It took Schulte about two minutes to unlock the iPhone. The developers would not give CNN their last names, saying "We don't want to be hounded." The said they would start selling the software, which they haven't yet priced, as soon as their online payment and customer service systems are ready. They're also waiting for more information from their lawyers. Apple spokeswoman Jennifer Bowcock told CNN her company has no comment. AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel said he couldn't speculate on the legality of unlocking the phone, but he added, "When you sign up, you're signing a two-year contract. You're obligated to pay the bill." "When people buy the iPhone it's clear from our materials it's designed to operate exclusively on AT&T," Siegel said. Schulte, however, said it is possible to buy an iPhone without being contractually obligated to AT&T. The developers recently created a Web site -- iPhoneSIMfree.com -- but there is very little information on it and no direct way for anyone to purchase the software. Internet records showed they bought the domain name less than two weeks ago. Two members of the group, who identified themselves only as "John" and "Liu," told CNN in a phone interview that a core group of six people on three continents worked to unlock the iPhone as a hobby. They said they are fans of Apple products who thought the iPhone should be made accessible to people who cannot use AT&T. "I'm not in America and I can't use it," said Liu, who would not reveal the country in which he lives. "It's not fair." Asked if he thought modifying the iPhone was legal, he said "That's a very good question. I truly believe it is." John and Liu said they have not been contacted by either Apple or AT&T, but said that could change the moment their software goes on sale. Earlier this month, a teenager figured out a way to unlock the iPhone, but his method required disassembly of the unit. E-mail to a friend .

**LOS ANGELES (CNN) —** A group of anonymous software developers says it will soon begin selling a program that allows iPhone owners to use the hugely popular device on cellular networks around the world, rather than exclusively with AT&T.

Apple’s iPhone, released in the United States two months ago, was engineered to operate for its first two years solely on the AT&T network under an exclusive agreement between Apple and AT&T. The device has not yet gone on sale outside the United States.

Los Angeles software consultant Brett Schulte, who is not affiliated with the developers, demonstrated the software for CNN on Friday evening. An iPhone running the new software appeared to connect to the T-Mobile network within seconds after Schulte replaced the AT&T SIM card with a T-Mobile SIM card.

“It’s completely software hacked,” Schulte said. “There’s no case opening required. It’s not required to do any kind of disassembly.”

It took Schulte approximately two minutes to unlock the iPhone.

The developers declined to provide CNN with their last names, saying, “We don’t want to be hounded.” They said they would begin selling the software—which they have not yet priced—as soon as their online payment and customer service systems are ready. They are also awaiting further information from their lawyers.

Apple spokeswoman Jennifer Bowcock told CNN that the company had no comment.

AT&T spokesman Mark Siegel said he could not speculate on the legality of unlocking the phone, but added, “When you sign up, you’re signing a two-year contract. You’re obligated to pay the bill.”

“When people buy the iPhone, it’s clear from our materials it’s designed to operate exclusively on AT&T,” Siegel said.

Schulte, however, said it is possible to purchase an iPhone without being contractually obligated to AT&T.

The developers recently created a website, iPhoneSIMfree.com, but it contains very little information and offers no direct way to purchase the software. Internet records show that they acquired the domain name less than two weeks ago.

Two members of the group, who identified themselves only as “John” and “Liu,” told CNN in a telephone interview that a core team of six people across three continents had worked to unlock the iPhone as a hobby. They said they are fans of Apple products who believed the iPhone should be accessible to people unable to use AT&T.

“I’m not in America and I can’t use it,” said Liu, who declined to reveal the country in which he lives. “It’s not fair.”

Asked whether he believed modifying the iPhone was legal, Liu replied, “That’s a very good question. I truly believe it is.”

John and Liu said they had not been contacted by either Apple or AT&T, but acknowledged that this could change once their software goes on sale.

Earlier this month, a teenager devised a method for unlocking the iPhone, but his approach required disassembling the device.

LOS ANGELES (CNN) — Anonymous programmers say they are preparing to sell software that would free iPhone users from relying solely on AT&T, allowing the popular handset to operate on mobile networks worldwide.

The iPhone debuted in the United States two months ago but has not yet been released in other countries. Under an exclusive agreement between Apple and AT&T, the device was designed to work only with AT&T during its first two years.

On Friday evening, Los Angeles software consultant Brett Schulte, who has no connection to the developers, showed CNN how the program works. After removing the AT&T SIM card from an iPhone and inserting one from T-Mobile, he demonstrated that the handset appeared to connect to T-Mobile within seconds.

The unlocking process took Schulte approximately two minutes and required no physical alterations to the phone.

“The hack is done entirely through software,” Schulte said. “You don’t have to open the case or take anything apart.”

The developers declined to provide CNN with their surnames because, they said, they did not want to face persistent attention. They plan to begin offering the software once their online payment and customer-support operations are functioning. They have not yet determined a price and are also awaiting additional legal advice.

Apple spokesperson Jennifer Bowcock said the company had no response. AT&T spokesperson Mark Siegel would not offer an opinion about whether unlocking the device is legal, but emphasized that customers who enter a two-year agreement remain responsible for paying their bills.

AT&T’s promotional information makes it clear that the iPhone is intended to operate exclusively on its network, Siegel added. Schulte, however, said consumers can purchase an iPhone without becoming contractually bound to AT&T.

The programmers recently launched iPhoneSIMfree.com, although the website contains little information and does not yet provide a direct purchasing option. Internet registration records indicate that the domain was acquired less than two weeks ago.

During a telephone interview with CNN, two members of the team identified themselves only as “John” and “Liu.” They said a central group of six people located across three continents had pursued the iPhone-unlocking project as a hobby. As admirers of Apple products, they believed the handset should also be available to people who cannot access AT&T’s service.

“I’m outside America, so I can’t use it,” said Liu, who refused to identify his country of residence. “That isn’t fair.”

When asked whether altering the iPhone was lawful, Liu replied, “That’s a very good question. I honestly believe it is.”

Neither Apple nor AT&T had contacted John or Liu, they said, though they acknowledged that the situation might change as soon as the software becomes commercially available.

Earlier in the month, a teenager discovered another method for unlocking the iPhone, but that approach involved taking the device apart.

Email this article to a friend.

A group of anonymous developers says it has created a software-only method for unlocking Apple’s iPhone, which was originally sold in the United States for exclusive use on AT&T’s network. Unlike earlier hardware-based techniques, the proposed hack would not require owners to open the phone, solder components, or make any physical modifications. After running the unlocking software, a user would reportedly need only to replace the AT&T SIM card with one from another compatible GSM carrier.

During a demonstration, an unlocked iPhone accepted a T-Mobile SIM card and connected to the carrier’s network within minutes. The phone was then able to operate without AT&T service, suggesting that the same approach could allow customers in other countries to use local GSM providers. Compatibility would still depend on the carrier’s network technology and supported radio frequencies, and some features—particularly data and carrier-specific services—might require additional configuration or function differently.

The developers reportedly intend to sell the unlocking software rather than release it publicly. If reliable, the tool could broaden the iPhone’s appeal by giving users more freedom to choose a carrier, avoid international roaming charges, or use the device in markets where Apple had not yet arranged an official network partnership.

However, the hack also raises unresolved legal and contractual issues. Unlocking could violate AT&T service agreements, affect Apple’s warranty coverage, or prompt the companies to disable the method through future software updates. Laws governing phone unlocking and circumvention technology also vary by country. As a result, prospective users would need to weigh the convenience of carrier choice against the possibility of technical problems, lost support, or legal disputes.

**LOS ANGELES, California (CNN) —** A group of programmers says it has found a way to unlock Apple’s iPhone using software alone, allowing the device to operate on T-Mobile’s U.S. wireless network.

In a demonstration in Los Angeles, representatives of iPhoneSIMfree.com inserted a T-Mobile SIM card into an iPhone originally restricted to AT&T. After running the group’s unlocking software, the handset connected to T-Mobile and was able to place and receive calls and send text messages.

The method does not require opening the phone or soldering its internal components, the group said. Earlier attempts to free the iPhone from AT&T’s network involved complicated hardware modifications that could permanently damage the $499-to-$599 device.

Apple introduced the iPhone in June under an exclusive U.S. agreement with AT&T. Buyers are required to activate the phone through Apple’s iTunes software and sign up for an AT&T service plan.

The software unlock could make the phone more attractive to travelers and customers who do not want to switch carriers. But in the United States, T-Mobile’s data network uses the same slower EDGE technology supported by the first-generation iPhone. Some AT&T-specific services, including visual voicemail, may not work on another network.

The group did not immediately release the software directly to the public, saying it planned to distribute the technology through resellers.

Neither Apple nor AT&T had confirmed that the unlock would continue to work after future iPhone software updates. Apple could change the handset’s firmware, potentially disabling unlocked phones or requiring users to repeat the process.

Unlocking also raises questions about warranties and service agreements. Apple has warned that unauthorized modifications may leave an iPhone inoperable and may not be covered by the company’s warranty.

Still, the demonstration marks a significant challenge to the tightly controlled business model surrounding one of the year’s most closely watched consumer products. For the first time, an iPhone appeared to be operating on a competing U.S. carrier without any physical alteration to the handset.

**Anonymous Team Plans to Sell Software That Unlocks Apple’s iPhone**

*Tool could let owners use carriers other than AT&T, but warranties, contracts and anti-circumvention law remain at issue.*

An anonymous six-person development team says it has created software capable of unlocking Apple’s iPhone and plans to sell the technology through third-party distributors, potentially allowing customers to use the device on wireless networks other than AT&T’s.

The group, known as iPhoneSIMfree, says its software removes the carrier restriction built into the original iPhone without requiring users to open the handset or modify its hardware. Technology publications that were given demonstrations reported that unlocked phones could make calls using non-AT&T SIM cards.

The developers have not publicly identified themselves, citing legal and commercial concerns. They also have not announced final pricing, instead saying the software would be licensed to resellers.

If widely released, the tool could weaken a central feature of Apple’s U.S. iPhone business model. Apple launched the phone under an exclusive agreement with AT&T, and buyers were expected to activate service with the carrier.

Apple cautioned that it had not authorized unlocking programs and that modifying an iPhone could leave it inoperable or affect its warranty. The company also retained the ability to change the phone’s software through updates, raising the possibility that an unlocked device could stop working after an upgrade.

AT&T likewise said customers were bound by the terms of their service agreements and warned that unauthorized alterations could void warranties or interfere with service. The carrier did not endorse the software and maintained that the iPhone was intended for use on its network in the United States.

The planned sale also raises unsettled legal questions. A U.S. Copyright Office exemption permits consumers, in certain circumstances, to bypass software locks on mobile phones to connect to another carrier. Unlocking advocates say that exemption supports a customer’s right to choose a network.

However, legal specialists note that the exemption does not necessarily resolve every issue. Distributing or selling circumvention software may be treated differently from an individual unlocking a phone, and users could still face claims involving copyright, licensing terms or breach of contract. Laws also vary outside the United States.

The developers say the process is reversible and does not alter the iPhone’s hardware. But until the software is released and tested more broadly, questions remain about its reliability, its compatibility with future Apple updates and whether Apple or AT&T will pursue technical or legal measures to stop its distribution.
